name: The lacuna between individual self-interest and the general happiness
plain_explanation: If Bentham is right that every person always pursues his own pleasure, it is unclear why a lawmaker, who is also just a person pursuing his own pleasure, would ever legislate for everyone else's happiness rather than his own.
precise_definition: The unresolved tension in Bentham's system between his psychological claim (each individual always pursues his own perceived happiness) and his ethical claim (the legislator's task is to secure the general happiness), which Bentham's own instinctive benevolence concealed from him rather than resolved.
why_it_mattered: Russell treats this as an 'obvious lacuna' at the heart of the whole Benthamite project, one that a more disillusioned age (Russell's own) can see was answered too optimistically by faith in democracy and supervision alone.
examples: Bentham's hope that democracy plus adequate supervision would force legislators to serve the public interest in order to serve their own
objections: Russell calls Bentham's optimism about democratic self-correction 'somewhat naive' in the light of subsequent experience
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Bears directly on the theoretical justification of representative democracy.
